meta.description: Chanel really said it. Quote Investigator traces the exchange to Haedrich's 1971 book from Chanel's tapes; the famous English wording is Markmann's 1972 translation.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Where should one use perfume? Wherever one wants to be kissed'?
meta.ogDescription: Documented: Haedrich's Coco Chanel secrète (1971), p. 201, and Markmann's 1972 English translation, p. 165. Earliest printing: Boston Globe, Dec 1962.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1883–1971 · French couturière, founder of the House of Chanel
answer.sourceLine: The exchange is printed in Marcel Haedrich’s Coco Chanel secrète (Robert Laffont, 1971), the book he built from Chanel’s own tape-recorded recollections; the familiar English wording is Charles Lam Markmann’s 1972 translation, Coco Chanel: Her Life, Her Secrets, page 165. A shorter version was already in print in The Boston Globe in December 1962, credited to “Mlle. Chanel” while she was alive.
answer.confidenceText: Chanel’s remark is documented — but the exact English sentence you see quoted is a translator’s, not hers. She said it in French.

source.excerpt: ‘Where should one use perfume?’ a young woman asked. ‘Wherever one wants to be kissed,’ I said.
trail: December 1962 — first known printing. Quote Investigator’s earliest evidence is a short columnist’s item in The Boston Globe of 27 December 1962: “A woman should use perfume wherever she wants to be kissed” … Mlle. Chanel. Chanel was alive and back at work in Paris. Quote Investigator ↗

1971 — the French book. Marcel Haedrich, editor in chief of Marie-Claire, encouraged Chanel to record her life story on tape and published Coco Chanel secrète from it. Page 201 carries the exchange in French: “Là où vous voulez vous faire embrasser, répondit Coco.” The book appeared in 1971, the year Chanel died. Verified with scans by QI ↗

1972 — the English wording everyone quotes. Charles Lam Markmann’s translation, Coco Chanel: Her Life, Her Secrets (Little, Brown), renders it on page 165 as ‘Where should one use perfume?’ … ‘Wherever one wants to be kissed.’ The Internet Archive’s catalog record confirms the translator and the 1972 edition. Internet Archive record ↗

The verdict. Quote Investigator concludes that Chanel deserves credit for the remark, naming the 1962 newspaper version and the 1971 French version as the two substantive candidates for the original phrasing — a rare clean result among Chanel attributions, many of which the same site opens with “Apocryphal?” among the candidates and closes without finding support. QI’s Chanel file ↗
source.excerptNote: In the book the reply is followed by Chanel’s own commentary on it: she says she saw the answer printed everywhere, found it a bore, and reckoned it earned her the friendship of the American reporters because she had told them something that made everyone laugh. In Haedrich’s French the exchange runs “— Où faut-il se parfumer? demanda une jeune femme. — Là où vous voulez vous faire embrasser, répondit Coco.”

author.name: Coco Chanel
author.heading: Who was Coco Chanel?
author.metaLine: 1883–1971 · French couturière & founder of the House of Chanel
author.bio: Gabrielle Bonheur “Coco” Chanel was a French fashion designer and businesswoman who opened a millinery boutique at 21 rue Cambon in 1910 and went on to make sporty, casual chic the feminine standard of style after the First World War. Her fragrance Chanel No. 5, launched in 1921, turned a couture house into a scent empire and made her a permanent fixture of the perfume press. She is the only fashion designer on Time’s list of the 100 most influential people of the 20th century.

misattribution.heading: The wording drifts — the attribution holds
misattribution.intro: This is the rare famous-name quote that survives investigation. What does not survive is the wording: almost every version shared online is a newspaper paraphrase rather than the sentence printed in the book, and the remark has also travelled with no name on it at all.

items.who: “A woman should wear perfume wherever she wants to be kissed”
items.why: The most-shared English form is not the 1972 translation. Quote Investigator records “A woman should use perfume wherever she wants to be kissed” in The Boston Globe of 27 December 1962 and “A woman should wear perfume wherever she wants to be kissed” in The Sun-Herald of Sydney in 1997 — both credited to Chanel, neither matching the book. Quote Investigator ↗
The “expects” phrasing appears in Quote Investigator’s 1973 Chicago Tribune citation, where it is presented as a general French belief about perfume with no speaker named at all. Quote Investigator ↗

Quote Investigator lists the actress and beauty author among the candidates because a 1975 Associated Press feature carried her line that French women place perfume on the parts of the body where they want to be kissed. She framed it as a French custom, and QI’s conclusion credits Chanel, not Dahl. Quote Investigator ↗

A Wikiquote editor filed the line under a “Perfume” heading on the Chanel talk page asking whether it was spurious, and no one answered; Wikiquote’s Chanel page still carries no perfume quote in any section. Wikiquote talk page ↗

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator’s verdict is that Chanel deserves credit for the remark, with the 1962 newspaper version and the 1971 French book both substantive candidates for the original phrasing — so quote it as hers, but know that the English you are quoting is Charles Lam Markmann’s. See the full chronology ↗

context.heading: Why the line stuck
lead: Chanel launched Chanel No. 5 in 1921, and from then on every interviewer wanted her on the subject of scent. The perfume quip is her answer to that recurring question — and in Haedrich’s book she is quite unsentimental about it, noting that she watched the reply get reprinted everywhere and that it won her the friendship of American reporters precisely because it made everyone laugh.

The remark sits in the chapter Haedrich calls “The Sixth Victory: The Comeback,” the account of Chanel’s return to couture after her 1954 collection. That placement fits the paper trail: the earliest printing Quote Investigator found is a December 1962 Boston Globe item, during her comeback years and well within her lifetime — she died in Paris on 10 January 1971.
context.detailsSummary: Why the version you have seen probably isn’t the book’s
detailsBody: The wording that circulates on social media — “A woman should wear perfume wherever she wants to be kissed” — is not the sentence in the 1972 translation. It is the newspaper form: the 1962 Boston Globe ran “A woman should use perfume wherever she wants to be kissed,” and The Sun-Herald of Sydney printed “wear” in 1997. Both are credited to Chanel; neither is the book.

The “expects to be kissed” variant has a separate paper trail. Quote Investigator’s 1973 Chicago Tribune citation presents it with no name attached at all — as a general French belief that perfume “should be applied wherever a woman expects to be kissed.”

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's earliest evidence is a 27 December 1962 Boston Globe item, page 19: "A woman should use perfume wherever she wants to be kissed" ... Mlle. Chanel.

Marcel Haedrich, editor in chief of Marie-Claire, encouraged Chanel to use a tape recorder to describe her life story, and in 1971 published Coco Chanel Secrète (Éditions Robert Laffont, Paris), chapter 14, page 201, containing "— Où faut-il se parfumer? demanda une jeune femme. — Là où vous voulez vous faire embrasser, répondit Coco." (verified with scans by QI).

The 1972 English translation by Charles Lam Markmann, Coco Chanel: Her Life, Her Secrets (Little, Brown and Company, Boston), chapter 14 "The Sixth Victory: The Comeback", page 165, renders it: "'Where should one use perfume?' a young woman asked. 'Wherever one wants to be kissed,' I said." followed by Chanel's remark that she saw the answer printed everywhere, it was a bore, but it earned her the friendship of American reporters (verified with hardcopy by QI).
QI's conclusion: "QI believes that Coco Chanel deserves credit for this remark. The phrasing of the 1962 version and the 1971 French version are both substantive candidates."

A 1973 Chicago Tribune column (18 Feb 1973, p. C10) printed the remark with no speaker named: perfume "should be applied wherever a woman expects to be kissed"; a 1975 AP feature quoted Arlene Dahl saying French women place perfume on parts of the body where they want to be kissed; The Sun-Herald (Sydney), 6 July 1997, printed "A woman should wear perfume wherever she wants to be kissed," said Coco Chanel.

Internet Archive holds a borrowable scan of "Coco Chanel, her life, her secrets" by Marcel Haedrich, translated by Charles Lam Markmann, 277 pages plus plates, a translation originally published Boston: Little, Brown, 1972, of the French "Coco Chanel secrète" (Paris: Laffont, 1971).

Coco Chanel (Gabrielle Bonheur Chanel) was born 19 August 1883 in Saumur, France and died 10 January 1971 in Paris; she was a French fashion designer and businesswoman, opened a millinery boutique at 21 rue Cambon in 1910, launched Chanel No. 5 in 1921, staged her comeback collection in 1954, and is the only fashion designer on Time's list of the 100 most influential people of the 20th century.

The Wikiquote talk page for Coco Chanel contains, under a "Perfume" section, an unanswered editor question: "What about 'A woman should wear perfume wherever she wants to be kissed.'? Is it spurious?"
Wikiquote's Coco Chanel page contains no quote about perfume and being kissed in any of its sections (Quotes, Quotes about Chanel, External links).

Quote Investigator's Coco Chanel tag index lists multiple other Chanel inquiries whose candidate line includes "Apocryphal?" as one of the options (e.g. "Fashion Is Always a Reflection of the Time", "Fashion Is Architecture", "In Order To Be Irreplaceable One Must Always Be Different"); "Apocryphal?" appears only inside those candidate question lists, never as a stated verdict — this article's own line reads "Coco Chanel? Arlene Dahl? Apocryphal?" and QI nonetheless credits Chanel.
